entries.name: The Transylvanian Unitarian Church, 1660 to 1906
entries.statusDescription: Proposed for a future survey, as a register entry. By its own pastor's statement of 1875, it reads as stepping outside the doctrinal floor. The question is not decided yet. Not yet reviewed.
entries.sourcing:
Moderate, and almost all of it the church's own voice. The Library holds two books by József Ferencz: a short history in Hungarian from 1875 and an English account of 1907. This entry uses the account of 1907 only for events up to 1906. Thomas Rees, an English Unitarian, wrote about the exile from Poland in 1818.

No Catholic source and no Latin or Hungarian archive was read, so the seizures of 1693 and 1716 are told as the Unitarians told them. The sources give different years for some events, and this entry says so. The scan of the Hungarian book has accent errors.
entries.floorNote: In 1875 their pastor József Ferencz wrote that the Unitarian faith denies the Trinity. In his words, it holds neither Christ nor the Holy Spirit equal to God. He calls Jesus a perfect man and the greatest of the prophets. This is the church's own account, not a charge made by its opponents. Whether it places them outside the floor is not yet decided. Noting this is not a judgment on what was done to them. Poland drove out its Unitarians in 1660, and in 1716 an army commander took their main church at Kolozsvár by force.
entries.relationsSummary: This entry carries on the Unitarian church told in the entry for 1517 to 1650. In 1660 Poland drove out its Unitarians, and some joined this church at Kolozsvár. Ferencz says the Jesuits took its college and its main church. American Unitarians were in touch with it from 1868, and English Unitarians from 1821.
entries.why: In 1660 Poland told its Unitarians to turn Catholic or leave. Some came to Kolozsvár, where the church that Ferenc Dávid had led still stood. Under Austrian rule from 1691 the church lost its college and its main church. In 1848 it won lawful standing, and in 1861 it chose a bishop again.
entries.teaser: Transylvania, 1660 to 1906. A small church took in Poland's exiles, lost its college and main church to Habsburg rule, and won full legal recognition in 1848.
entries.longDescription:
In 1658 the Diet of Warsaw brought a formal charge against the Polish Unitarians, the English Unitarian Thomas Rees wrote in 1818. A decree then banned their public worship on pain of death. It told them to leave Poland within three years, unless they joined the Catholic, Lutheran or Calvinist church.

József Ferencz, a Unitarian pastor at Kolozsvár, dates the ban to 1659. Rees and Ferencz both put the order to leave in July 1660, though they give different days.

Rees says about four hundred went to Transylvania and Hungary. Ferencz says about 380 set out for Hungary. At the border, robbers took all they had.

Some settled in Hungary. Thirty to forty families went on to Transylvania. Their brothers in the faith took them in with love.

Most of them settled at Kolozsvár. There they founded a separate Polish church under the Transylvanian bishop.

They still worshipped in Polish around 1792. Their last pastor was Izsák Száknovics. Later they merged with the Hungarian congregation.

Pál Augustinovics was a descendant of the exiles from Poland. In 1837 he left his whole estate to the church.

Bishop Dániel Beké served until 1661. János Járai held the seat from April to June of that year. The seat then stood empty for two years, because the wars made church meetings impossible. Boldizsár Koncz was bishop from 1663 to 1684.

In 1691 Transylvania stopped being a separate principality and came under the Austrian emperor. In 1693 the Unitarians had to give up their old college at Kolozsvár, which had been theirs since 1566. Ferencz's account of 1907 says the Jesuits fell upon it.

A fire in 1697 burned down part of the church and its buildings. The church restored them. Pál Dimény, the head teacher, collected 9,000 thalers for this from Remonstrant and "collegian" brothers in Belgium and Holland.

On 30 March 1716 an army commander named Steinville took the market church by force. On 2 April a Catholic bishop led worship in it. The bishop's house, the school, the suburban church of Saint Peter and all their property were taken next.

More churches were lost, among them Torda in 1721 and Brassó in 1777. Under Charles III and Maria Theresa the Unitarians were slowly shut out of every public office. Their equal rights in religion were denied, and their writing was held back.

Mihály Szentábrahámi Lombárd led the rebuilding. His contemporaries said he was the eyes, heart and mouth of the Unitarians. In 1718, with nine students, he opened the church's third college. He was bishop from 1737 to 1758.

In 1791 László Zsuki gave the church all the capital he had gathered, and named the Kolozsvár college in particular. The college building of 1806 rose from his gift. The new Kolozsvár church, beside the college, was opened on 14 December 1796.

In 1848 the diet gave the Unitarian faith lawful standing. Ferencz calls this a worthy mark of respect for 300 years of struggle.

After Bishop Sándor Székely died in 1852, the government in Vienna would not let the church fill his seat. The seat stayed empty for nine years, and the government threatened to close the church's schools. In 1858 English Unitarians came to its aid with 13,000 forints. On 2 July 1861 the synod at Torda elected János Kriza bishop.

In 1868 the church marked 300 years, and the diet voted it a grant of 5,000 forints a year. On 13 June 1869 it held its first public service in Budapest, in a hall that the Reformed brothers lent. The census of 1869 counted 53,539 Unitarians in Transylvania and 788 in Hungary.

Ferencz says English Unitarians first wrote to Kolozsvár in 1821, and the church wrote back. His account of 1907 gives the year 1822. In 1830 and 1847 young men preparing to teach went in person to London.

In 1831 Sándor Bölöni Farkas toured North America. He was the first to make the Hungarian church known to the Americans.

In 1868 the Americans sent a greeting for the church's 300th year. Dall, their missionary in India, also came to Kolozsvár.

Ferencz says Dall won American help to translate Channing's works into Hungarian. He says it was given. By 1873 American friends were raising money for two chairs at the Kolozsvár college, to be named for Channing and Priestley.

In 1875 Ferencz wrote that the Unitarian faith differs from other forms of Christianity above all in denying the Trinity. He wrote that it holds neither Christ nor the Holy Spirit equal to God. He calls Jesus the greatest of the prophets, the Christ or Messiah, God's holy son, and a perfect man. He adds that the church does not claim to be infallible.

entries.legacy:
Ferencz's account of 1907 calls it the Unitarian Church of Hungary, and names Ferenc Dávid as its founder. The tree has no entry for it after 1906.

The tree also has no entry yet for the English Unitarians after 1813, the Dutch Remonstrants after 1650, or the Reformed church of Hungary after 1815. This entry tells their ties to this church in words only.
